doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Deciding on music and rejecting classical
summary: Music chose her around college; classical felt too tight; she was a music jock in high school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: When was it that you decided that, you know music is going to be it for me? Was it kind of a decision that came early, junior high?

Well it was never a question in my mind that I was a musician from the earliest memories that you could have as a kid. I can remember being fascinated with musical instruments, I mean now I’m talking really early. I knew I loved music and it was clear very early on that I had a special feeling for it. I started studying piano and drums and saxophone when I was very young. And it just took a while for me to realize that that’s what I was going to do for a living. I think it was around college time. It became clear to me that that was the only thing I could do. I didn’t really have a choice. Basically you find out it chooses you.
If I don’t do music, humm, what can I do, right?
I couldn’t think of anything I could do better than play. And when I understood what it meant to be a performer and what I brought to it and what it felt like doing it.
Was there ever an indication that you might go in the classical field of music?

I remember looking at that possibility once. Because of course studying the saxophone you had to learn how to produce sound on the instrument much in the way any classical artist might study an instrument. But I don’t know, even as a kid I think I had a sense that that wasn’t for me, that the parameters for how you had to express yourself were a little too tight for me. I didn’t feel I could express myself in that genre really.
Well you know when you think of the field of classical saxophone, it would be a little tough to make a living, probably harder than jazz. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Probably so. But you know also there was a sense, even as a kid I understood the sensibility about the freedom that was involved in expressing yourself as a jazz player. That was more in keeping I think with my personality.
Did you establish a reputation in high school as a little bit different because you were a jazz saxophone player?

Whatever I was, yeah I was definitely different. I was definitely a music jock and no question about it, I marched to a different drummer in my younger years. But I guess I just felt this passion to study music and to play, and I guess at that time that makes you different from how you spend your free time than other kids spend their free time.
